questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals() for Strings?
questions.title: == vs .equals() for Strings
questions.direct_answer: == checks if two references point to the same object; .equals() checks if two Strings have the same character content.

interviewer_intent.testing: The most common Java trap — every interviewer asks this
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == for String comparison in code, or not being able to explain why
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete example showing when == unexpectedly returns false

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: In Java, == on any object tests reference equality — are these two variables pointing to the exact same memory address? .equals() tests content equality — do these two strings contain the same characters? For Strings, you almost always want content equality.

The == trap: if (status == "active") seems to work in tests because your string literal gets pooled. But when status comes from a database or HTTP request it's a new object — == returns false even though the content is identical. That's a real production bug.

sections.hook: Every Java interviewer asks this. It's not just theory — using == on Strings causes real production bugs.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So == on any object in Java checks reference equality — are these two variables pointing to the exact same object in memory? .equals() checks logical equality — do these two objects have the same content?

With String literals, == often returns true because of the string pool. `"hello" == "hello"` is true because both reference the same pooled object. But this creates a trap: if either String comes from a variable, method call, or new String(), == can return false even when the content is identical.

The rule is: always use .equals() to compare String content. Never rely on == for Strings. A common real-world bug is doing `if (status == "active")` — this seems to work during testing because your literal gets pooled, but breaks at runtime when status comes from a database or HTTP parameter.

For null-safe comparison, use `Objects.equals(a, b)` or `"literal".equals(variable)` — the second form works because calling equals on a literal can't throw NullPointerException even if variable is null.

sections.title: Key Points
content: == on Strings causes real production bugs

questions.question: What does String.compareTo() return and when do you use it?
questions.title: String.compareTo()
questions.direct_answer: compareTo() returns 0 if equal, negative if the string comes before the argument lexicographically, and positive if it comes after.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of String ordering and sorting
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking compareTo() returns boolean or forgetting the sign convention
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention it implements Comparable<String> which is why Strings sort naturally in TreeSet/TreeMap

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: compareTo() compares two strings lexicographically — dictionary order based on Unicode values. It doesn't return a boolean. It returns an int: zero means equal, negative means this string comes first, positive means it comes after the argument.

content: String implements Comparable<String> — so TreeSet and TreeMap sort strings automatically

beats.content: The practical use case is sorting. Collections.sort() on a List<String> uses compareTo() under the hood. compareToIgnoreCase() works the same way but ignores case — useful when sorting user-visible strings.

sections.hook: compareTo() doesn't return true or false. It returns a number — and the sign of that number tells you everything about the ordering.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So compareTo() compares two strings lexicographically — basically dictionary order based on Unicode values. It returns three possible outcomes: zero if the strings are equal, a negative number if this string comes before the argument, or a positive number if this string comes after.

The exact return value is the difference in char values at the first position where they differ. So `"apple".compareTo("banana")` returns a negative number because 'a' < 'b'. `"cat".compareTo("cat")` returns 0. `"zoo".compareTo("apple")` returns positive.

The main use case is sorting. String implements Comparable<String>, so TreeSet and TreeMap sort strings automatically using compareTo(). When you use Collections.sort() on a List<String>, it uses compareTo() under the hood.

There's also compareToIgnoreCase() which does the same thing but ignores upper/lower case differences.

sections.title: Key Points
content: 0 = equal, negative = comes before, positive = comes after
TreeSet/TreeMap use compareTo() for natural ordering

questions.question: What are the common String search methods — contains(), startsWith(), endsWith()?
questions.title: String Search Methods
questions.direct_answer: contains() checks if a substring exists anywhere; startsWith() and endsWith() check the beginning and end; indexOf() returns the position.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that contains() takes a CharSequence not just String, or not knowing indexOf() returns -1 for missing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show awareness of the full family of search methods and their return types

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Java's String search API has two tiers: boolean methods for quick yes/no checks, and indexOf() for when you need the position.

rows: Is this substring anywhere in the string?
Does the string begin with this?
Does the string end with this?

beats.content: Quick tips: contains() takes a CharSequence, not just String — a StringBuilder works too. indexOf() returns -1 when not found, not null or false. contains(s) is exactly equivalent to indexOf(s) != -1. Use contains() when you only need a yes/no answer — it reads more clearly.

sections.hook: Java has a whole family of String search methods. Know which one returns a boolean and which one returns a position.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Java has a clean family of String search methods. `contains(CharSequence s)` returns true/false — does this string contain s anywhere? `startsWith(String prefix)` checks the beginning, `endsWith(String suffix)` checks the end. These three return booleans and are easy to use.

`indexOf(String s)` is more powerful — it returns the index of the first occurrence, or -1 if not found. You can also use `indexOf(String s, int fromIndex)` to search from a specific position. `lastIndexOf()` searches from the end.

`matches(String regex)` checks the whole string against a regex pattern. `regionMatches()` compares substrings between two strings without creating substring objects.

A practical tip: `contains()` is equivalent to `indexOf() != -1`. For simple checks, contains() reads more clearly.

sections.title: Key Points
content: indexOf() → int position or -1 if missing

questions.question: How do you compare strings case-insensitively in Java?
questions.title: Case-Insensitive Comparison
questions.direct_answer: Use equalsIgnoreCase() for equality or compareToIgnoreCase() for ordering — both are safer than toLowerCase().equals() due to locale issues.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Turkish locale 'I' problem with toLowerCase()

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: The go-to method is equalsIgnoreCase(). It checks whether two strings have the same characters regardless of case, with no locale surprises. For sorting case-insensitively, use compareToIgnoreCase().

content: equalsIgnoreCase(str) — safe, no locale dependency, always prefer this
compareToIgnoreCase() — for ordering and sorting without case sensitivity
Avoid toLowerCase().equals() — lowercase conversion is locale-sensitive
Turkish locale trap: toLowerCase() turns capital I into a dotless lowercase i, so "TITLE".toLowerCase(Locale.TURKISH).equals("title") returns false

beats.content: For sorting a list of strings ignoring case, pass String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER as the comparator to Collections.sort().

questions.question: How do you compare strings safely when one might be null?
questions.title: Null-Safe String Comparison
questions.direct_answer: Use Objects.equals(a, b) or put the literal first — 'literal'.equals(variable) never throws NullPointerException even if variable is null.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling variable.equals('literal') when variable could be null
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show Objects.equals() and explain both null returns false, both null returns true

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: If you call variable.equals("active") and variable is null, you get a NullPointerException. Two patterns avoid this cleanly.

content: Objects.equals(a, b) — null-safe: both null returns true, one null returns false, both non-null compares content
"active".equals(variable) — Yoda condition: the literal can never be null, so no NPE even if variable is null
variable.equals("active") — unsafe if variable might be null, avoid this
Objects.equals() is the most readable option for production code

beats.content: In practice, Objects.equals() is what most teams use. It handles every null combination correctly and reads like normal equality.

sections.hook: One line — variable.equals("active") — NPEs if variable is null. Two patterns fix it completely.
